chunks.heading: Who he is
chunks.text: I'm a Generative AI Engineer at Virtusa. I build agentic harnesses for work that cannot afford to be wrong quietly: legacy reverse engineering, Spring Boot migration and vulnerability remediation. Each one follows the same pattern. Deterministic analysis comes first, governed model reasoning second, everything is traceable, and a person approves before anything ships. I have five years in machine learning and NLP, the last two on production LLM systems in enterprise modernisation, financial risk and healthcare.

chunks.heading: How he frames the work
chunks.text: Most AI work fails at the engineering layer, not the model layer. A capable model behind a weak pipeline is still a demo: it drifts, it can't be evaluated, and nobody can tell you why it answered the way it did.

chunks.heading: Current focus
chunks.text: Open to Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Applied AI Engineering roles. Based in Denton, Texas. Currently Generative AI Engineer at Virtusa, since Jun 2026.

chunks.heading: Structured contracts over prompt hacks
chunks.text: A model that returns free text is an integration problem waiting to happen. I design schemas first and constrain generation to fit them, so downstream systems get something they can validate instead of something they have to parse.

chunks.heading: Retrieval you can trace
chunks.text: Grounding is only useful if you can show your work. I separate retrieval, reasoning, and validation into distinct stages so every answer carries its evidence, which also makes failures diagnosable instead of mysterious.

chunks.heading: Evaluation before scale
chunks.text: Hallucination rate, answer accuracy, and latency are engineering metrics, not vibes. I build the measurement harness before the system grows, because you cannot improve a pipeline whose behaviour you are guessing at.

chunks.heading: Cost and latency are features
chunks.text: Token spend and p95 response time decide whether a system is adopted or quietly switched off. I profile both from the start and treat a regression in either as a bug, not a trade-off to explain away.

chunks.heading: MARS
chunks.text: An agent harness that takes a reported Java vulnerability from diagnosis to a scored ship decision. Agents judge; scripts decide. Built in 2026. Domains: Agentic AI, Multi-agent, Legacy modernisation, Migration, Evaluation. Stack: Node.js, JavaScript, TypeScript, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot Chat, OpenRewrite, Maven, Neo4j (optional), tree-sitter, React.

chunks.heading: MARS: the problem
chunks.text: Writing a security patch is the easy part. What takes time is everything after it: does the patch close the finding, can a different path still reach it, did it change behaviour nobody asked to change, does it build, and who decided it was safe to ship? A coding assistant asked to "fix this CVE" answers all of those in one confident paragraph. The paragraph cannot be audited, and nothing in it separates what was measured from what was guessed.

chunks.heading: MARS: approach
chunks.text: Split the work across seven agents in three phases, Understand, Fix and Verify & Ship, with eighteen skills between them. Each skill is a self-contained folder of scripts, JSON schemas and policy data. Gave every agent the same division of labour. Deterministic scripts collect facts into a briefing, the agent writes its judgement into a schema-checked JSON file, and a renderer merges the two into the Markdown report the next stage reads. Required a human-approved fix plan before any code is written. Stage 1 of the fix agent writes a plan and is not allowed to write a patch. The implementing scripts read only plans whose Status cell is Approved. Ran every patch in a temporary git worktree or a sandbox copy, and let exit codes, not the agent, decide whether tests and builds passed. Moved the ship decision into a config-driven scorer. scoring.json defines three hard gates (still vulnerable, build failed, migration not passed) and per-severity thresholds. An agent may override a computed Cleared to Blocked. It cannot go the other way. Built the migration skill to plan Spring Boot upgrades edge by edge over a 17-rung ladder. Its licence policy refuses source-available recipes unless an opt-in is recorded. Added Mission Control, a React operations console fed by a telemetry ledger. A run can be watched there, and the plan decision can be recorded through the same guarded command the terminal uses.

chunks.heading: MARS: architecture
chunks.text: Seven agent personas run in order inside a coding-assistant session (Claude Code or GitHub Copilot Chat). Each one calls deterministic Node.js scripts for facts and writes its judgement into schema-checked JSON. Then a renderer merges the two into a report. Two lines are enforced: no patch before a person approves the plan, and no agent can clear a patch that a script-computed gate blocked. Understand and plan: reads only (agents 01–04, stage 1): 01 Architect (Turns the codebase into an AST model, a Neo4j graph and architecture documents.) → 02 Root cause · 03 Blast radius (Scripts collect evidence from the graph and the code. The agent names one root cause and sizes its reach.) → 04 Strategize (Writes a fix plan, never code, and classifies it as a code fix, a dependency upgrade or a version migration.). Implement: only in an isolated worktree or sandbox (agent 04, stage 2): Plan approval (A person moves the plan from Proposed to Approved. The implementing scripts read only that cell.) → 04b Fixer · 04c Upgrader · 04d Migration (The agent drafts the smallest patch. Scripts apply it in a temporary git worktree and verify that it compiles.). Verify and ship (agents 05–07): 05 Re-scan · red-team · behaviour guard (Three static checks on each patch: does the finding still trigger, can it be bypassed, did behaviour change?) → 06 Test gate · build gate (Runs one new regression test and the full build in a worktree. The exit codes decide the result.) → 07a Merge arbiter (Scores the evidence against severity thresholds and applies three hard gates that no score can override.) → 07b Verdict, PR text and audit trail (Writes the PR content and the audit record. Opens a PR only for a Cleared patch, and only when a person asks.)

chunks.heading: MARS: Scripts measure, agents judge, renderers merge
chunks.text: The model is good at explaining why a defect is real and bad at reporting whether a build passed. So no agent ever writes a test result or a build verdict: a script runs the command and records its exit code, and the report renders that number. Agent judgement goes only into JSON that has to validate against a schema, which is what lets every report show the measured facts and the judgement side by side.

chunks.heading: MARS: An override can only make the verdict stricter
chunks.text: Agent 07 may disagree with the score, but in one direction only. The verdict renderer refuses an override unless the computed decision was Cleared and the override sets it to Blocked. A persuasive narrative can stop a patch. It cannot ship one.

chunks.heading: MARS: The approval is recorded, and the record admits its limits
chunks.text: Approval began as a hand edit of a Markdown cell, which records nothing about who approved, when, or which version of the plan they saw. record-decision.js now writes a hash-chained decision log and refuses a stale plan, a non-interactive terminal, and a Claude Code process. Its own header says attribution is locally asserted: a process running as the same OS user could defeat it. The checks deter, and the dashboard’s integrity rule detects. Neither proves.

chunks.heading: MARS: Licence is a policy input, not a footnote
chunks.text: rewrite-spring 5.24.1 is the last Apache-2.0 release of Spring’s upgrade recipes. Beyond Boot 3.3, the default open-source-only policy uses MARS’s own composites built from core OpenRewrite recipes, plus compiler-driven repair. A recipe the session’s policy does not allow is rejected with a recorded status. It is never quietly skipped or quietly used.

chunks.heading: MARS: measured results
chunks.text: 7 / 18 agents and skills, At 07c1644: ls .github/agents/*.agent.md | wc -l and ls -d .github/skills/*/ | wc -l. Matches the README badges. 24,137 lines of harness JavaScript across 86 files, plus 7,946 lines of TypeScript in Mission Control, At 07c1644: git ls-files on .github/**/*.js excluding tests, piped to wc -l. Excludes the .claude mirror and the vendored Spring Boot sample application. 56 harness test cases across 9 files, and 98 Vitest + 12 Playwright tests for Mission Control, At 07c1644: git grep -cE '^\s*(test|it)(\.each\(…\))?\s*\(' on *.test.js / *.test.ts(x) / *.spec.ts. Static count, not run. All 56 harness tests cover two skills, 04a routing and 04d migration. 3 hard gates that no score can override, hard_gates in .github/skills/07a-merge-arbiter/scoring.json, enforced in compute-score.js before the threshold is applied. 0 of 4 committed sample issues cleared to ship, Decision row of docs/agent_output/07-ship/verdict_ISSUE-00{1..4}.md at 07c1644. All four are Blocked, with scores of 0, 30, 60 and 60.

chunks.heading: MARS: known limitations
chunks.text: Sixteen of the eighteen skills have no automated tests. The harness tests cover fix-plan routing and the migration skill only. There is no CI. The repository’s only Jenkinsfile belongs to the sample application under analysis and checks out a different repository. The README says MARS can migrate Spring Boot from any published line to any later line. The ladder does describe 17 lines from 1.5 to 4.1, but the committed validation exercises two paths: 2.7.12 → 3.5.16 (partial pass) and 3.5.0 → 4.1.1. A bypass does not block on its own. BYPASS_FOUND caps the score at 70, which is above the Low-severity threshold of 65, so a Low-severity patch with a known bypass can still be Cleared. The README lists this as an open problem. Agent 02 has no "not a defect" outcome. Every issue in the register is treated as real. In the validation runs, plan approvals were given programmatically. The human checkpoint exists in the design and was not exercised by a person in those runs. Some committed sample reports were edited by hand after rendering. The README warns that re-scoring them would wrongly clear two issues. The .claude copy is a hand-maintained mirror of the .github harness, and 42 of its 80 JavaScript files are not byte-identical to a .github counterpart. The two drift by construction.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway
chunks.text: Three agents negotiate what data a risk question actually needs, and the layer that reasons never holds a database credential. Built in 2026. Domains: Agentic AI, Multi-agent, MCP, RAG, Evaluation. Stack: Python, MCP, A2A, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Qdrant, Redis, React, TypeScript, LangSmith.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: the problem
chunks.text: "What is the 10-day 99% VaR on this book?" is three questions wearing one coat. One is methodological and its answer lives in a risk corpus, not a database. One is a capability question: a par yield curve carries no instrument identifiers, so any method needing them is simply unanswerable against this data. Only the third is retrieval and arithmetic. The obvious architecture, user to model to unrestricted SQL to a dump of rows, fails all three at once: it loses the quoting basis, recalls parameters from training that nobody can falsify, returns nine thousand dates when asked for a curve, has no way to refuse, and runs with a credential that is one bug away from writing to the source of record.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: approach
chunks.text: Split the work across three agents addressed over A2A (an orchestrator, a domain expert, and an agent that owns tool access), each advertising its skills on a card, with requests refused if they name a skill the card does not carry. Put a free pre-flight gate in front of everything: regular expressions and a lexicon decide in under a millisecond whether the question is complete enough to be worth a model call. Grounded methodology in two retrieved corpora, then required every figure in the derived plan to appear verbatim in a retrieved passage. A number the model produced but cannot point at fails the check. Made the domain expert and the tool agent negotiate the data requirement over at most five rounds, terminating early if two rounds change nothing, and allowed the outcome to be a refusal. Narrowed 56 underlying MCP tools down to 34 advertised capabilities, because a planner choosing under uncertainty gets worse with every near-duplicate option it is offered. Split data access from computation into two MCP servers: the data server holds a read-only Postgres role; the risk engine holds no credential, no model and no network, and a test asserts that no module inside it imports a database driver. Returned bulk numeric data out of band rather than through model context: a 250-day matrix is 1,250 values, and a truncation partway through would corrupt a result silently rather than loudly.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: architecture
chunks.text: Three bands, read left to right. The agents understand the question, negotiate what data would actually answer it, and only then execute, across a boundary they never cross themselves. Every agent in the first two bands reasons; none of them holds a database credential. Understand: before anything is retrieved: Pre-flight gate (Regex and lexicon decide whether the question is answerable at all.) → Orchestrator (Classifies the turn into an eight-field structured contract.) → Grounded retrieval (Two Qdrant collections behind an exact-key Redis lookup.) → Domain Expert: derive (Proposes a data requirement, then checks its own figures against the source.). Negotiate: bounded, and allowed to fail: MCP Agent: capabilities (Advertises 34 capabilities, narrowed from 56 underlying tools.) → Bounded negotiation (At most five rounds, and at most two that change nothing.). Execute: Data MCP server (14 tools over Postgres, holding a read-only role.) → Risk engine MCP server (42 tools. No database credential, no model, no network.) → Validate & answer (Checks the result, strips identifiers, assembles a cited reply.)

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: Two MCP servers, split by failure attribution
chunks.text: When a VaR number looks wrong there are exactly two possible causes: bad input, or bad arithmetic. With the split, each is checkable on its own: replay the same payload through the engine, or query the data server for provenance. Combined into one server, you are guessing. This is the boundary the product is built on rather than an implementation detail.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: The reasoning layer holds no credential
chunks.text: The risk engine is launched with a sanitised environment containing no connection string, and its own module documentation lists what is deliberately absent: any database driver, any language model, any network access. It has to return the same number every time, and a model anywhere in that path would make the claim untrue.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: Documentation drift is treated as a failing test
chunks.text: When a document claims five risk tools and the server registers forty-two, the count is not merely stale; it is evidence nobody reconciled the two. So the authoritative inventory is derived from the registered tools at test time and the documents are checked against it, never the reverse.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: Strict validation because a silent wrong answer is the worst outcome
chunks.text: A renamed field parses cleanly and turns into a null three layers downstream, where it is indistinguishable from a legitimate absence. Structured output is validated against its schema strictly and loudly, on the principle that a loud failure costs a retry and a quiet one costs trust in every number the system has ever produced.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: measured results
chunks.text: 1,839 tests, collected and counted rather than estimated, pytest --collect-only against a clone, with the dependency floors the project actually pins. 267,517 rate observations across 52 series, 1990 to 2026, Recounted directly from the committed source CSVs without a database, and matched to the documented figure exactly. 56 MCP tools registered (14 data, 42 risk), narrowed to 34 advertised, Both servers booted locally and list_tools() called; counts are what the servers actually return. 13 × 11 evaluation grid: cases scored against graders including groundedness and refusal, Read from the harness: graders include rows_are_grounded, no_ungrounded_numbers and impossible_fields_refused. ~53,900 lines of Python across 175 files, plus 6,488 of TypeScript, Counted by directory; the figure excludes nothing and includes the 13,383 lines of tests.

chunks.heading: Semantic MCP Data Access Gateway: known limitations
chunks.text: The container build is broken. It copies a path that a refactor moved, so it fails on the first instruction, and even repaired, it installs three of the five distributions. There is no working containerised deployment today. One of the two model backends cannot plan a data request at all. Its schema caps are lower than the planning contract requires, and no arrangement of the parameters satisfies both. This is recorded as a strict expected-failure so that it will fail loudly if it is ever silently "fixed". A fully negotiated turn takes between 110 and 370 seconds and makes six to thirteen model calls. This is a reasoning system, not an interactive one. Session memory is an in-process dictionary. A restart loses every conversation. There is no authentication. Allow-lists authorise against caller-supplied metadata, which is not a security boundary. The demonstration portfolio is a single synthetic five-position book, labelled as synthetic end to end. The VaR figures are an analytical demonstration, not a regulatory calculation. No CI. The test suite is substantial and nothing runs it automatically.

chunks.heading: Bootshift
chunks.text: A Spring Boot migration harness that refuses to claim more than it verified. Built in 2026. Domains: Agentic AI, Multi-agent, Legacy modernisation, Migration, Evaluation. Stack: Java 21, Maven, OpenRewrite, JavaParser, JGit, ArchUnit, Jackson, Picocli.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: the problem
chunks.text: A Spring Boot major upgrade is not a version bump. It changes the namespace from javax to jakarta, the security configuration model, the Java baseline, the auto-configuration mechanism, hundreds of property names and the whole transitive dependency graph, at once. The tools that exist answer "it compiles." The question a team actually has is "does it still do the same thing?" Nothing answers that, so the work falls back on manual review of a diff nobody can hold in their head.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: approach
chunks.text: Split the pipeline into twenty stages across three phases, with eleven read-only analysis stages that must complete before anything is permitted to write. Routed every source modification through one FileMutationGateway, and enforced that with an ArchUnit rule that walks bytecode for direct filesystem calls from the transformation packages, so "only the gateway writes" is a property the build checks, not a convention. Made every change append to a hash-chained ledger, including rejected ones, so the record of a run covers what was refused as well as what was applied. Froze the migration plan (edge order and per-edge validation depth) before the first write, so the harness cannot lower its own bar once an edge gets hard. Declared the old-versus-new comparison as a contract up front: each dimension is MUST_MATCH, EXPECTED_TO_DIFFER or UNCONSTRAINED, and a dimension that could not be compared is reported NOT_COMPARED rather than passed. Kept the optional AI provider restricted to a loopback address and off by default, with seven tests asserting the boundary. It can suggest a repair; it cannot authorise one.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: architecture
chunks.text: The pipeline condensed to its three phases. Eleven analysis stages read but never write; six stages repeat per migration edge and are the only ones permitted to change source; three finalise. Every write in the middle band passes through a single gateway. Analysis: read-only (11 stages): Inventory & build resolution (Reads the repository and resolves what the build actually declares.) → Application graph (Builds the static structure: types, beans, configuration, dependencies.) → Baseline capture & seal (Records pre-migration behaviour, then seals it. No stage may write before this.) → Impact & characterization (Predicts what the upgrade touches and captures current behaviour as tests.) → Migration plan: frozen (Fixes the edge sequence and each edge’s validation depth before any write.). Per migration edge: the only stages that write (6 stages, repeated): Transformation (Applies one recipe per batch, each computed against the current file hash.) → FileMutationGateway (The single chokepoint every source write passes through.) → Build, test & runtime validation (Rebuilds, reruns tests, and starts the services to observe real behaviour.) → Differential validation (Compares old against new on pre-declared dimensions.). Finalization (3 stages): Approval (Decides between completion, a policy block, and escalation to a human.) → Evidence & provenance (Seals the report, the SBOM and the provenance graph.)

chunks.heading: Bootshift: File identity is allocated, not derived
chunks.text: Path identity breaks the moment SecurityConfig.java is renamed; content-hash identity breaks on the first edit. A migration is precisely the operation that changes both, so each file gets an allocated ID that survives rename, split and merge, which is what makes the change ledger traceable across the whole run.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: Validated artifacts outrank the state machine
chunks.text: The run state says where the pipeline is; versioned artifacts say what is true. When they disagree, state is reconstructed from the artifacts and never the other way round. Writes advance a `latest.json` pointer only after schema validation passes, so a half-written artifact is never the one a later stage reads.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: The graph is rebuilt in full every edge
chunks.text: Incremental update is much faster and is the classic source of silent drift, and the failure is invisible precisely because the mechanism that would detect it is the thing that broke. Reversing this decision is gated on a test asserting the incremental graph equals the full rebuild.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: One recipe per batch, each pinned to a base hash
chunks.text: An earlier version batched recipes. Two of them targeting the same pom.xml were both computed from the pre-edge file, so the second write silently discarded the first, and the ledger recorded both as applied. Now a stale base hash is rejected outright.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: measured results
chunks.text: 35,928 lines of harness code across 140 files, git ls-files on the six Maven modules; excludes the sample Spring Boot application the harness analyses. 191 test methods across 21 test classes, Static count of @Test at HEAD. The README says 143; the README undercounts two suites and omits five classes entirely. 20 pipeline stages: 11 analysis, 6 per-edge, 3 finalization, Read from PipelineOrchestrator, not from the documentation. 542 property-migration rules, generated rather than hand-written, rule_count in migration-rules/generated-properties/property-migration-rules.json. 1 of 8 migration edges completed on the reference run before it halted, reports/BOOTSHIFT_FINAL_IMPLEMENTATION_AND_PIPELINE_REPORT.json.

chunks.heading: Bootshift: known limitations
chunks.text: No migration has been carried through end to end. On the reference corpus the run completed one of eight planned edges and then halted on a policy block: one configuration property appeared only in the new build and the cause could not be verified. That is the designed outcome, the harness will not manufacture an explanation: but it means the system is demonstrated, not proven in production. Stages 18 to 20 are written and wired but have never been executed by a completed run, so they are unverified in practice. Runtime validation can only characterise what it can start. On the reference corpus one of six modules never starts, and that gap is emitted as a named blind spot rather than hidden. There is no CI in the repository. The test suite is real and runs locally; nothing runs it automatically. No kernel-level sandbox: a malicious Maven plugin the repository already trusts would run with the harness’s privileges.

chunks.heading: Statute
chunks.text: Reverse-engineers an undocumented Oracle PL/SQL system into a requirements document, with no language model anywhere in the generation path. Built in 2026. Domains: Reverse engineering, Legacy modernisation, Evaluation. Stack: Python 3.11, ANTLR4, sqlglot, Mermaid, Neo4j (optional).

chunks.heading: Statute: the problem
chunks.text: An organisation runs a working system whose documentation is missing and whose authors have left. Before it can be modernised, replaced or audited, somebody has to answer what it does and which rules it enforces, and the only remaining authority on that is the source. The tempting approach is to point a language model at the code and ask. The reason not to is specific: a deterministic extractor that misses a rule fails visibly, and a generative one that invents a rule fails invisibly. In a document that will be used to rebuild a system, an invented rule is worse than a missing one, because nothing downstream will question it.

chunks.heading: Statute: approach
chunks.text: Built eight independent CLI programs chained by versioned JSON artefacts on disk: no orchestrator, no shared state, no service, so any stage can be rerun and inspected on its own. Parsed with a formal Oracle PL/SQL grammar and decomposed SQL with a dedicated library, so structure is derived rather than guessed. Assembled every sentence of the document by rule from the resulting parse trees, which is what makes the same source produce the same document every run. Extracted business rules from nine distinct kinds of evidence (conditional branches, named and predefined exceptions, CASE branches, variable derivations, check constraints, cursor eligibility, failure isolation and error contracts), and graded each by confidence. Recorded a disabled database constraint as not enforced, rather than presenting it as an active business rule. Marked each requirement’s modality: a constraint the database enforces is necessary; a guard in application code is obligatory. Separated the diagram model from the diagram renderer after the previous inline version proved untestable, which took that stage’s checks from 7 to 52.

chunks.heading: Statute: architecture
chunks.text: Oracle PL/SQL becomes a business requirements document, diagrams and a knowledge graph. Every stage is an independent CLI program chained by versioned JSON on disk; the structure comes from a formal grammar and every sentence is assembled by rule. 1 · Inventory (Classifies the source files and assigns each a stable identifier.) → 2 · Parser (A formal PL/SQL grammar produces statements and a control-flow graph.) → 3 · Data (Turns DDL into a schema model, its enforcement state, and an ERD.) → 4 · Logic (Pseudocode, two complexity metrics, and program slices.) → 5 · Rules (Extracts business rules from nine distinct kinds of source evidence.) → 6 · Diagram (Builds a diagram model, then renders it as a separate step.) → 7 · Synthesis (Assembles the document, marking each requirement’s modality.) → 8 · Graph (Emits a loadable knowledge graph for querying the result.)

chunks.heading: Statute: No model call anywhere, as the central thesis
chunks.text: This is the decision the project exists to test. Because nothing generates text, hallucination is not reduced; it is structurally unavailable, which is what makes it safe for every claim in the output to cite a source line. The recorded cost is stated just as plainly: prose quality is bounded by the quality of the templates, and the naming heuristics took substantial iteration to get right.

chunks.heading: Statute: Two complexity metrics, and one deliberately rejected
chunks.text: McCabe measures testability and Cognitive Complexity measures understandability; they answer different questions and both are reported. The Maintainability Index was rejected because its volume term has no consensual definition, and because averaging complexity hides exactly the power-law outliers where the real risk lives.

chunks.heading: Statute: Identity hashes the path, not the contents
chunks.text: A file identifier derived from contents changes on the first edit, which breaks traceability precisely when a document is being maintained. Hashing the path keeps identity stable across edits, which is what lets a requirement still point at its source after the code moves on.

chunks.heading: Statute: measured results
chunks.text: 414 assertions across eight suites, all passing, All eight suites run locally and PASS lines counted. These are assertions, not test functions; the suites use a custom check harness. Zero language-model imports anywhere in the repository, Searched every module for every major LLM SDK. No matches, and no network, environment or database imports in the pipeline either. 41 business rules and 21 recorded gaps extracted from the reference corpus, Read from the generated artefact, alongside a 2,549-line requirements document. 0.588 rule-extraction F1 on blind measurement, with 0.400 recall, The tuned figure is 1.000 and the project disowns it: ground truth was used to fix the extractor, so only the blind numbers are reported here.

chunks.heading: Statute: known limitations
chunks.text: The extraction F1 the harness prints is contaminated: the ground truth was used to fix the extractor. Only the blind figures (0.588 F1 and 0.400 recall) are defensible, and they are the ones published above. It has only ever been run against a single banking corpus of five objects and fifteen tables. It has never been pointed at unfamiliar PL/SQL. Coverage metrics demonstrate completeness, not usefulness. A document can cover every branch and still fail to explain the business. Concepts cannot be recovered from code. What the pipeline produces are solution and functional requirements; genuine business requirements are not recoverable from an implementation. One relationship type is computed by the diagram stage and never emitted by the graph stage; the loop that would write it is empty. There is no dependency manifest, no CI, no container and no logging framework.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness
chunks.text: Scores legacy code on twenty complexity dimensions, and refuses to return a number when it is missing the inputs. Built in 2026. Domains: Agentic AI, Legacy modernisation, Migration, Evaluation. Stack: Python 3.11, Standard library only, unittest.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: the problem
chunks.text: The project began with a defect that did not raise an error. Feeding one analyzer a tree built in another analyzer’s format produced "units seen: 0" and a clean-looking result. Worse, several analyzers ignored their file argument entirely and printed complete reports from hardcoded demo data, confirmed by handing one a file declaring an invented language and getting a report about Java back. Running the full suite would have produced seven genuine results and thirteen fabricated ones, with nothing on the page distinguishing them.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: approach
chunks.text: Defined one language-neutral Normalized Tree and made every analyzer read only that, never source text, so an analyzer cannot be fed a format it does not understand. Moved input validation into a single gate that runs before any analyzer function is called. An analyzer starved of its declared inputs returns insufficient_input naming the gap, and physically cannot return a zero instead. Made analyzer discovery a filename glob over the skills directory, so nothing anywhere holds a list of the twenty and adding a twenty-first requires no edit elsewhere. Banded results L1–L5 against language-aware thresholds rather than reporting raw scores, because the same cyclomatic number means different things in different languages. Required corroboration before flagging a hotspot: a unit is only a hotspot when two or more independent analyzers band it L4 or L5, since a unit flagged by one analyzer is usually that analyzer’s bias. Built an adversarial judge with ten checks, and a deliberately defective canary analyzer that the judge must flag as critical or the self-test fails.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: architecture
chunks.text: Three agents drive three deterministic scripts; a fourth stage runs only when a target migration language is named. The gate before stage 3 is the design’s whole point: an analyzer missing its declared inputs returns “insufficient_input”, never a zero. Stage 1: Inventory (Declaration-only scan. Never enters a method body.) → Stage 2: Parser (Hand-written tokenizer builds the language-neutral Normalized Tree.) → The input gate (Checks each analyzer’s declared inputs before it is allowed to run.) → Stage 3: Complexity (Discovers, orders, gates, runs and merges twenty analyzers.) → Stage 4: Target fit (Projects the tree onto a target language and re-runs the same analyzers.)

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: Absence of measurement and absence of complexity are different facts
chunks.text: This is the rule the whole harness rests on. A zero is a claim about the code; insufficient_input is a claim about the harness. Conflating them is what made the original defect invisible, so the distinction is enforced centrally rather than documented as guidance.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: The auditor has to be capable of failing
chunks.text: The judge passed all twenty analyzers on its first run, which is equally consistent with a judge that cannot detect anything. So a canary analyzer with five planted defects was added. It caught four and missed one: and the miss is what produced a tenth check, which then immediately found two real defects in shipped analyzers that read line counts they never declared.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: Unreviewed language descriptors are penalised numerically
chunks.text: A drafted target-language profile scores 0.6 against a reviewed one’s 1.0. All five shipped descriptors are currently marked unreviewed, so the project applies the penalty to itself rather than exempting its own defaults.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: measured results
chunks.text: 20 / 20 dimensions measured on the reference tree; 18 of 20 on the committed Java runs, Reproduced locally: run_pipeline.py against samples/cobol_payroll.tree.json. The two unmeasured dimensions on the Java runs are named and explained rather than scored. 21 unit tests, all passing in 0.11s, python -m unittest discover, run, not counted. They cover stage 4 only; the analyzers are verified by the judge instead. 0 third-party Python dependencies, Every top-level import across all 37 .py files enumerated; all are standard library. 4 of 5 planted defects caught by the judge’s self-test, tools/judge.py --self-test reproduced locally: 20 pass, 1 critical, canary correctly flagged.

chunks.heading: Adaptive Legacy Complexity Harness: known limitations
chunks.text: Band calibration is judgement, not measurement. The thresholds reflect published practice and field experience, not a statistical study of a corpus. A tree is only as good as its parser: an insufficient_input result often indicates a parser gap rather than clean code. Stage 4 has no adversarial judge yet. It is covered by the twenty-one unit tests and nothing more. Only three fields of the target-language descriptor actually drive projection. Richer fields are read by the written report but carry no score impact, so a codebase relying on fixed-point arithmetic gets no penalty for that risk yet. There is no CI. The checks are manual, and they are the only thing between a defect and main.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge
chunks.text: Natural-language business intelligence over any PostgreSQL database, with the model boundary drawn deliberately. Built in 2026. Domains: Agentic AI, Multi-agent, Evaluation, Data engineering. Stack: Python, Streamlit, PostgreSQL, asyncpg, Redis, Plotly, Presidio, GPT-5.2, Claude Haiku 4.5.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: the problem
chunks.text: Ad-hoc business questions queue behind whoever can write SQL. The obvious fix, put an LLM in front of the database, fails in a specific way: it works against the schema it was demonstrated on, and breaks against the next one. It also tends to be built as one model call doing everything, which makes the output impossible to explain when a stakeholder asks why a particular chart was chosen or where a number came from.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: approach
chunks.text: Split the turn into nine stages with a typed contract between each, so a failure in one degrades the response instead of ending it. Put a zero-cost classifier in front of every model call, so greetings and non-data messages never reach a paid API. Discovered the schema at runtime through a single tool boundary over asyncpg, which is what lets the same deployment answer questions about an unfamiliar database. Wrote a deterministic SQL builder that assembles a valid aggregate query from the schema alone, used whenever generation fails, so a rate limit produces a narrower answer rather than an error message. Kept chart selection, aggregation and response assembly entirely in code: field profiling, candidate generation, a constraint engine and a scoring pass. Those stages make no model call at all. Separated statistical detection from narration: findings are computed, and the model is only asked to phrase them, because a model asked to find a pattern will report one whether or not it is there. Made the guardrail fail closed and every other stage fail open, then cached generated SQL in Redis against a fingerprint of the schema so a schema change invalidates it automatically.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: architecture
chunks.text: A question in English becomes a chart and a written finding. The stages shaded as model calls are the only ones that reach an LLM; chart selection, aggregation and response assembly are plain code, which is why they cost nothing and behave identically on every run. Synchronous: the user is waiting: Pre-classifier (Decides whether the message is a data question at all. No model call.) → Guardrail (PII redaction, rate limiting, and a safety decision.) → Intent & clarification (Classifies what is being asked; asks at most one clarifying question.) → SQL generation (Discovers the live schema, plans a query, validates and executes it.) → Visualization (Profiles the fields, scores candidate charts, builds the figure.) → Insight detection & narrative (Detects statistical findings deterministically, then writes them up.) → Composer (Assembles the reply. No model call.). Background: after the reply is sent: Memory (Extracts durable context for later sessions.) → Quality scoring (Scores the turn with a rule-based and LLM hybrid.)

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: Two stages that look like model work are not
chunks.text: Chart selection and response assembly are the stages most systems hand to an LLM. Both are deterministic here. Choosing a chart is a constraint satisfaction problem over field types and cardinality: code does it more cheaply, more consistently, and can explain the choice afterwards.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: One fail-closed stage, the rest fail open
chunks.text: The guardrail is the only stage where an exception produces a refusal. Everywhere else an exception produces an empty typed object and the turn continues, because a missing insight panel is a degraded answer while an unscreened query is a different category of problem.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: Evaluation runs after the user has their answer
chunks.text: Memory extraction and quality scoring are offloaded to a daemon thread with its own event loop. Scoring a response is genuinely useful and genuinely slow; making the user wait for it would trade the thing they asked for against the thing they did not.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: measured results
chunks.text: 95 / 110 tests passing with no database, cache or API key present, pytest run locally against a clone; the remaining failures need live PostgreSQL and Redis, except one genuine logic defect in the volatility detector. 78 source modules, 15,619 lines excluding tests, Counted across the repository, tests excluded and reported separately. 3 of nine stages reach a model; the rest are deterministic, Traced from the orchestrator through every reachable call site.

chunks.heading: DecisionForge: known limitations
chunks.text: The repository is private, so nothing on this page can be independently verified by a reader. The figures above were computed against a clone, and that is the only assurance available here. Per-stage cost and latency figures exist in the project’s own design notes but were never measured: no benchmark was run and no results were recorded, so none of them are reproduced here. PII redaction fails open: if Presidio is unavailable the text passes through unchanged. That is the wrong default for a production deployment and is a known gap rather than a decision. One statistical detector does not fire on its own test input. The test is correct and currently fails. Vector columns are declared in the schema but no embedding is ever computed, so there is no semantic memory despite the table supporting it.

chunks.heading: Graph-RAG clinical decision support for US hospitals

chunks.heading: Graph-RAG clinical decision support for US hospitals: the problem
chunks.text: Clinical decision support is the setting where a plausible-sounding wrong answer does the most damage. Pure vector retrieval over clinical text returns passages that read as relevant while missing the relationships that actually determine a diagnosis, which condition contraindicates which medication, which finding rules out which differential. Those are edges in a graph, not similarities in an embedding space, and a system that only knows how to measure similarity cannot see them.

source.title: Graph-RAG clinical decision support for US hospitals

keywords: Graph-RAG clinical decision support for US hospitals

chunks.heading: Graph-RAG clinical decision support for US hospitals: approach
chunks.text: Unified a Neo4j clinical knowledge graph with FAISS vector search, so retrieval could follow explicit clinical relationships as well as semantic similarity. Put Azure OpenAI behind that retrieval rather than in front of it, keeping generation constrained to what the graph and the index actually returned. Integrated live EHR data through FHIR, so reasoning ran against the patient record in front of the clinician rather than a stale extract. Fine-tuned Long-T5 and BART on clinical corpora using PEFT/LoRA for the summarisation path, where a general-purpose model produced handoff notes that were fluent and incomplete. Built the intake side as a separate voice pipeline (Azure Speech-to-Text into LangGraph multi-agent orchestration, persisting to Cosmos DB), so capture and reasoning failed independently. Ran it all on zero-downtime MLOps: AKS, Azure ML, MLflow, Terraform and GitHub Actions, because a clinical service that needs a maintenance window is a clinical service people route around.

chunks.heading: Grounded research assistant for graduate coursework
chunks.text: A retrieval system over course materials and academic databases that answered students’ research questions with citations instead of guesses. At University of North Texas, 2024–2025.

chunks.heading: Grounded research assistant for graduate coursework: the problem
chunks.text: Graduate students repeatedly asked the same categories of research question: where to find a method, which database indexed a given journal, how a technique from lecture applied to their project. Faculty and teaching assistants answered each one individually. A general-purpose chatbot was worse than useless here: it invented citations, and in an academic setting a fabricated reference is a serious failure, not a rough edge.

source.title: Grounded research assistant for graduate coursework

keywords: Grounded research assistant for graduate coursework

chunks.heading: Grounded research assistant for graduate coursework: approach
chunks.text: Scoped the corpus deliberately to course materials and academic databases, over 10,000 documents, so every answer had a retrievable source rather than relying on model recall. Built the retrieval layer on FAISS for dense search with PostgreSQL holding document metadata and provenance, so each response could name where it came from. Ran hybrid dense-sparse retrieval through a LangGraph pipeline on Azure with sentence-transformer embeddings, holding sub-second responses under concurrent multi-user load. Used Redis for session state, which is what made multi-turn research conversations coherent: a follow-up question inherits the context of the one before it instead of starting cold. Tuned FAISS index parameters and added Redis caching against real student queries collected during the semester, rather than against a synthetic benchmark that would not reflect actual usage. Constrained generation to retrieved context and declined to answer when retrieval returned nothing relevant. Refusing is the correct behaviour when the alternative is a plausible-looking invented citation.

chunks.heading: Grounded research assistant for graduate coursework: architecture

Orchestrated with LangGraph on Azure.

chunks.text: Every new job posting on the marketplace started a manual shortlisting pass over more than twenty thousand candidate profiles. chunks.text: calmvoice: Text-or-voice wellbeing companion answering from a licensed corpus with citations, behind a crisis gate. cloudquote: Turns a plain-English infrastructure requirement into side-by-side AWS and GCP cost quotes. gadgetgenie: Text-to-SQL device recommender where code guards each generated query and checks every number in the summary. gradguide: Graduate advising assistant that answers from an institution's own documents with citations, or abstains. onboardiq: RAG assistant that answers a new data-team member's questions from team docs, filtered by role and level. paper2pod: Turns an arXiv paper into a multi-voice podcast WAV with a grounding and length quality report. truthtrace: Fact-checker that matches a political claim to PolitiFact and FactCheck.org articles or abstains. holisticare-rag: Local health Q&A assistant that answers from your own labelled documents with a checked citation per sentence. nutribuddy: Retrieval-grounded diet planner for diabetes, heart disease and thyroid disorders, with cited plans. reportwise: Explains lab report PDFs: rules flag abnormal values, then one LLM call writes a validated, cited explanation. studybuddy-rag: Study tutor that routes text or voice questions by subject and answers from course material with citations. symptom-sage: Symptom RAG over simulated doctor-patient interviews with red-flag triage and a medicine filter. vid2thumb: Turns a spoken video into a transcript, summary, generated thumbnail and the best real frame.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Agents & tool use
chunks.text: clinicdesk-agent: Tool-calling clinic assistant that books, cancels and reschedules only after patient confirmation. policypilot: Routes insurance questions to SQL, MongoDB or policy-document RAG agents behind query validators. retailia: Tool-using store assistant that scopes every data read to the signed-in customer and cites FAQ answers.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: LLM evaluation
chunks.text: citecheck: Benchmark of per-field hallucination and omission when an LLM writes academic references. ehr2summary: Generates cited discharge summaries from coded EHR tables and scores them with rules and a separate judge. emotune: Benchmark comparing baselines, zero-shot, few-shot and LoRA language models on 6-label emotion classification. paperdigest: Evaluation harness comparing paper summarizers and QA/RAG systems with confidence-interval leaderboards. resume-arena: Benchmark harness that compares LLMs and prompt styles on resume writing with faithfulness-aware metrics. dischargebench: Early-stage benchmark that prepares leakage-free MIMIC-IV note pairs for Brief Hospital Course summarization.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: NLP
chunks.text: biasradar: Text classifier that flags social-bias generalisations and scores 10 bias categories independently. culturefit: Recruiter review aid that matches a job's stated work values to a candidate's own words as quoted evidence. kindify: Toxic-comment classifier for the 6 Jigsaw labels that offers guarded polite rewrites of flagged comments. mindclassify: Benchmarks classifiers of mental-health posts across 7 labels, with calibration and a crisis-routing rule. reddit-pulse: Sentiment, aspect sentiment and topic pipeline for Reddit policy debates, validated against gold labels. sentiment-grid: Benchmark harness for three-class sentiment encoders and heads under one shared training protocol. snaptranslate: OCR translator for signs and menus that picks the OCR pack, detects language and routes to a backend. tweetmood: Tweet sentiment toolkit comparing lexicon, TF-IDF, hybrid neural and fine-tuned models on one shared split.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Medical imaging
chunks.text: cellsight: Five-class blood-cell image classifier with duplicate-aware splits and out-of-fold stacking. chestx-multitask: Patient-split benchmark kit for comparing image backbones on the 14 NIH ChestX-ray14 finding labels. colongrade: Grades ulcerative colitis colonoscopy images on the Mayo endoscopic subscore with patient-grouped folds. dermavit: Lesion-grouped, multi-seed benchmark comparing ViT-B/16 and Hiera-Base on HAM10000 skin-lesion classes. hepatoscan: Liver and tumor CT segmentation scored per volume, plus a cited, non-diagnostic patient assistant. lunglens: Calibrated malignancy estimate for one marked lung nodule on CT, with a fixed-template report in 94 languages. pneumovit-explain: Chest X-ray pneumonia classifier with patient-aware splits and explanations independent of its prediction.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Clinical ML
chunks.text: dementia-typer: Classifies OASIS-3 visits into five dementia groups from MRI volumes with participant-level splits. eeg-rx: Subject-wise nested evaluation of whether resting-state EEG features predict SSRI treatment response. fedsugar: Like-for-like benchmark of federated vs centralized training on BRFSS diabetes indicators. heartstack: Coronary artery disease risk models from three public cohorts with nested CV and leave-one-source-out. neurorisk: Tabular Alzheimer's risk models that separate risk-factor features from symptom features, with nested CV.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Computer vision
chunks.text: engagecam: Subject-disjoint benchmark that classifies face frames into 7 engagement states with a source-confound probe. leafdoctor: Plant-disease leaf classifier with CNN plus handcrafted features, leaf-grouped splits and a field test. paddyguard: Rice leaf disease classifier that tests whether lagged local weather adds value to image models. signsight: Traffic-sign classifier with a weather-corruption robustness benchmark and a latency report.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Forecasting
chunks.text: btc-gini-signal: Walk-forward ablation testing whether Gini and Kolkata inequality features improve Bitcoin return forecasts. ev-diffusion: Forecasts yearly EV adoption with Bass and Generalized Bass models and measures owner-review sentiment. firecast-id: Benchmark for 1- to 30-day forecasts of daily NASA FIRMS fire-hotspot counts in Indonesia. gridiron-oracle: Walk-forward NFL home-win probabilities from point-in-time features and pre-game Elo ratings. hotfood-forecast: Forecasts daily hot-food demand by category and turns quantile forecasts into newsvendor orders. skyfusion: Fuses ground-station and NASA POWER data to forecast hourly temperature 1 to 24 hours ahead.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Applied ML
chunks.text: ipm-lstm-attn: Learned Newton solvers for interior-point methods, compared in a seeded one-change-at-a-time ablation. autovalue: Calibrated price and delivery-time bands for a used-car marketplace, with an approve-or-review price rule. churn-colony: Telecom churn models with ant-colony feature selection and a profit-based contact threshold. crash-whatif: Crash-severity classifiers explained with permutation importance and actionable what-if counterfactuals. driverisk: Turns a raw telematics stream into trip rows and a per-driver risk index from harsh-event rates. roadrisk-live: Scores US accident severity with live OpenWeather data and backtests daily accident-count forecasts. salescope: Sales prediction for BigMart item-outlet data with CV that tests unseen outlets and unseen items. eta-eats: Food delivery time regression with checked category maps, time and courier splits, and a model card.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Recommenders
chunks.text: crossrec: Cold-start cross-domain recommender that suggests books from Amazon food ratings and food from book ratings. fridge2fork: Recipe recommender that ranks recipes for the ingredients you have and shows the real steps from the data. profmatch: Recommends professors from research profiles and smoothed teaching ratings, with reasons for each result. sensehome: Furniture recommender that fuses look, feel, text and sound features with modality attention. stylematch: Fashion recommender combining TF-IDF, BM25, dense and hybrid retrieval with an optional LLM re-ranker.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Speech & audio
chunks.text: speakright: Pronunciation coach that aligns recognised phones and Mandarin tones to the target and gives tips. callscribe: Diarization plus ASR pipeline that labels each word of a long earnings call with its speaker and scores it.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Analytics
chunks.text: ballots-to-markets: Event-study and Granger-test pipeline asking whether 2024 election news and Fed decisions moved U.S. markets. crashinsight: Survey-weighted injury-severity study of NHTSA GES crash data with crash-grouped model evaluation. riverpulse: Study toolkit for England river water quality: CCME index, weather effects and a COVID effect with intervals. shelf-to-screen: Builds a validated library-by-year panel from Texas library statistics to study the print-to-digital shift. dietverse: Country-level diet analytics, a personal diet guide and a key-safe backend for a VR nutrition assistant. telehealth-insights: Survey-weighted analysis kit for the NEHRS physician telemedicine survey with adjusted odds ratios. twitter-to-x: Before/after study pipeline for sentiment and moderation talk in posts around the Twitter-to-X change.

chunks.heading: Earlier work: Security
chunks.text: sast-vs-llm: Benchmark comparing static analyzers and LLM code reviewers on a labelled Python corpus.
